messages.subject: chat.nk application
messages.body_plain:
We used the chat.nk function to estimate overdispersion in a 3-year study on elk that we are doing.  We used the most global model and found no overdispersion for males during any year and overdispersion for females only during the last year of sampling.  The first 2 years had chat values close to 1.  My question is whether we should adjust all the SEs on D or just the last year?  Which chat should we used for the QAICc calculation?
Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: chat.nk application
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joe
c-hat is estimated with error. David Fletcher advises against applying a correction unless the calculated c-hat lies outside the range expected by chance. In the coming release of secr that can easily be checked by simulation (new argument 'nsim' in chat.nk() triggers simulations). Release is a week or two off; otherwise get the development version from GitHub.

If some sessions have significant overdispersion and others don't then my preference is to base the decision on biological judgement: adjust if it makes sense because you can see a biological explanation for the difference. At least we are just talking about CI width - not like the bad old days where CAPTURE had people jumping between 'preferred' estimators, with different biases.

QAIC: a very good question, and one I've asked David to think about. Possibly c-hat pooled (averaged) across sessions, but what should be the weights? Similar sample size would argue for equal weights.

As an early adopter you may have to be patient as we sort out the wrinkles!
Murray

messages.subject: Re: chat.nk application
messages.body_plain:
Sound like you are on it Murray, as usual.  The elk are gregarious animals of course but almost all the scats we collected were in and around relatively about 10 small fields in the area.  We used a distance to field covariate to account for that in the model.  My thought is that since the animals are grouped based on habitat patchiness, that the overdispersion caused by herding behavior is minimized.  We happened to have a couple of transects that last year that went right through an active elk herd so we got lots of samples in year 3 at that site.  I think that is accounting for a lot of the overdispersion we are getting that year..  My gut tells me that the CIs are not too narrow without adjusting with chat.

messages.subject: secr 4.6.0
messages.body_plain:
secr 4.6.0 is on CRAN, and the Windows binary will follow in a few days (see also GitHub <https://github.com/MurrayEfford/secr>).

This version has improved handling of large transect datasets (thanks to Philipp Jund for tweaks to C++ code).

Several functions extend the treatment of spatial overdispersion (c-hat across detectors). The coverage is not comprehensive (e.g. mixture models are excluded). This is an active area of research and it's too soon to give definitive advice.

messages.subject: different detector devices
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently working with a dataset analysing rat density with three trapping sessions, each of them with three occasions, . Trapping devices were mostly Tomahawk traps, but in certain cases these were complemented with other devices (e.g.,  Sherman traps and handmade traps). The latter show much lower CPUE than Tomahawk traps (0.07 captures/trap-night and 0.01 captures/trap-night vs. 0.20 captures/trap-night ), yet some individuals were caught with them. Considering the huge difference in capture probability, I would like to know if there is a way to indicate to the model that different detecteros were used, so that it takes into account the different detection probability. Alternatively, what would happen if I include these detectors without considering capture probability differences? I guess the detection function should  be affected but I would appreciate any indication, particularly regarding the density output. Thank you in advance.

Best

Julien

# test multi-session time-varying trap covariates
library(secr)

# generate some covariate data, assign separately for each session

for (sess in 1:5) {
rand <- sample.int <http://sample.int>(2,44,replace = TRUE)  # nonsense values, 44 nets

messages.subject: Combining data from different survey methods
messages.subject_clean: Combining data from different survey methods
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’m carrying out an analysis of lion density using two data sets: camera trap data from a camera trap survey, and direct sightings data from a search-encounter survey. Both the surveys were carried out in the same area and during the same period.

In addition to comparing the separate density estimates produced through these two survey types, I'd like to try and combine the different data types into a single model. This is because I expect it should improve my density estimate (by virtue of increasing the number of captures and recaptures), and more broadly because I think it could be a useful approach in certain contexts, and would like to work out how (if!) it can be done.

I’ve already modelled both these datasets separately in secr. For the camera trap data, I used proximity detectors with binary effort. For the search encounter data, I converted the study area into a 1x1km grid of cells, with effort calculated as the number of kilometres driven in that cell on that day – this means it is also proximity detector type, but with a different (non-binary) measure of effort.

I know that there is currently no function to pool capthist data from different detector arrays, and that it is recommended to merge the input files and rebuild the capthist object from scratch. However, is it possible to do this with two different survey methods with different measures of effort (binary and non-binary)?

Otherwise it would be possible to use a binary measure of effort for the search encounter data (i.e. 1 if that pixel was surveyed on that sampling occasion, 0 if it was not) and combine it with the camera trap data into a single set of input files. However, the actual effort is really quite different between the two data types, so this seems like it may not be a good way forward.

Any advice would be much appreciated!

Thanks,
Charlotte

'binary.usage' is an argument of read.traps that has no downstream effect, as I remember. Once upon a time, all 'usage' data were binary, then the capability expanded (the code in read.traps from 2012 is still marked as 'tentative'!). 'binary.usage' merely switches between old and new input code blocks. The usage matrix of a traps object can mix binary and non-binary.

So I suggest you simply enter the trap- and occasion-specific values together with binary.usage = FALSE. Use only spaces, not commas (until a fix I have just applied on GitHub percolates through to another CRAN version of secr).

Of course, you will need to model differing detection parameters.

Murray

On Saturday, May 27, 2023 at 2:50:43 AM UTC+12 charlott...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
> I’m carrying out an analysis of lion density using two data sets: camera trap data from a camera trap survey, and direct sightings data from a search-encounter survey. Both the surveys were carried out in the same area and during the same period.
>
> In addition to comparing the separate density estimates produced through these two survey types, I'd like to try and combine the different data types into a single model. This is because I expect it should improve my density estimate (by virtue of increasing the number of captures and recaptures), and more broadly because I think it could be a useful approach in certain contexts, and would like to work out how (if!) it can be done.
>
> I’ve already modelled both these datasets separately in secr. For the camera trap data, I used proximity detectors with binary effort. For the search encounter data, I converted the study area into a 1x1km grid of cells, with effort calculated as the number of kilometres driven in that cell on that day – this means it is also proximity detector type, but with a different (non-binary) measure of effort.
>
> I know that there is currently no function to pool capthist data from different detector arrays, and that it is recommended to merge the input files and rebuild the capthist object from scratch. However, is it possible to do this with two different survey methods with different measures of effort (binary and non-binary)?
>
> Otherwise it would be possible to use a binary measure of effort for the search encounter data (i.e. 1 if that pixel was surveyed on that sampling occasion, 0 if it was not) and combine it with the camera trap data into a single set of input files. However, the actual effort is really quite different between the two data types, so this seems like it may not be a good way forward.
>
> Any advice would be much appreciated!
>
> Thanks,
> Charlotte
